title: URL Shortener Design
description: Learn to design a scalable URL shortener service with hashing, base-62 encoding, distributed ID generation, and high-throughput redirect handling.

data.text: A URL shortener converts long web addresses into compact, shareable links. Services like Bit.ly and TinyURL handle billions of redirects daily. Designing one tests your ability to balance low latency, high availability, and storage efficiency while keeping links memorable and human-readable.

data.title: Core Features
items: Shorten a given URL and return a unique short link
Redirect a short URL to its original destination
Support custom aliases for branded links
Track click analytics and link expiration dates

data.title: Performance and Reliability
items: Redirect latency must be under 100 ms to avoid perceived slowness
System must remain available even during partial outages
Links should expire gracefully with configurable TTL

data.text: Most URL shorteners use base-62 encoding because it produces compact, URL-safe strings without reserved characters. The character set is 0-9, a-z, and A-Z, giving 62 options per character. With just 7 characters you can encode over 3.5 trillion unique IDs. An auto-incrementing numeric ID from a database or ID generator is converted into a base-62 string to form the short code.

data.title: Why Base-62?
data.text: Base-62 is shorter than hexadecimal (base-16) and avoids URL-unsafe characters present in base-64 (such as +, /, and =).

The system uses a stateless API layer behind a load balancer, a distributed ID generator, and a key-value store for fast redirects. The write path stores the mapping in a database and caches it in Redis. The read path checks Redis first, falling back to the database on a cache miss. A CDN or edge cache can serve hot redirects without hitting your origin servers.

data.title: Prevent collisions
data.text: Always validate short code uniqueness at write time. Even with a perfect ID generator, concurrent requests can theoretically collide. Use a unique constraint on the short_code column and handle duplicate key errors gracefully by retrying with a new ID.

terms.definition: A numeral system using 62 characters (0-9, a-z, A-Z) to encode numbers into short, URL-safe strings.
A service that produces unique identifiers, such as auto-incrementing sequences or distributed algorithms like Snowflake.
A test short link used to monitor redirect latency and detect degradation before user traffic is affected.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Base-62 encoding produces compact, URL-safe short codes
Use a key-value store like Redis for redirect caching to meet sub-100ms latency
Choose an ID generator based on write volume and coordination complexity
Enforce uniqueness with database constraints and handle collisions via retries
data.takeaway: A successful URL shortener hides complexity behind a 7-character redirect while serving millions of requests per second.

items.question: How do you handle analytics without slowing redirects?
items.answer: Log the redirect event asynchronously to a message queue. A separate analytics service consumes events and updates counters. This decouples analytics from the critical redirect path.

items.question: What happens when a short link expires?
items.answer: Return a 404 or redirect to an expiration notice page. Delete expired entries from the cache to free memory and serve accurate results.

data.title: Practice Estimation
data.description: Estimate storage and QPS for a URL shortener with 50 million daily active users, each creating 2 links per day and clicking 15 links per day.
data.expectedOutcome: Write QPS ~ 1,160; read QPS ~ 17,361; ~5 TB storage per year assuming 500 bytes per entry
